## Performance Showdown
When you’re weighing a **gaming laptop vs desktop**, raw power is usually the first thing that comes to mind. Desktops have historically held the edge because they can house larger, more robust components without worrying about thermal throttling or battery life. A full‑size tower can accommodate a high‑end CPU, a top‑tier GPU, and plenty of RAM, all cooled by spacious airflow or liquid‑cooling loops. This translates into higher sustained frame rates, the ability to push graphics settings to ultra, and smoother performance in CPU‑intensive titles like simulation or strategy games.

Laptops, however, have closed the gap dramatically. Modern gaming laptops pack mobile versions of the same GPUs found in desktops—think RTX 40‑series or RX 7000‑series—paired with powerful CPUs like Intel’s 13th‑gen HX series or AMD’s Ryzen 7000H/HS chips. While they can’t always match the absolute peak of a desktop counterpart due to power limits, many laptops deliver excellent 1080p and even 1440p gaming at high refresh rates. The trade‑off is often a slight dip in sustained performance during long gaming sessions, but for most players the difference is negligible in everyday use.

### CPU and GPU Power
Desktops benefit from larger dies and higher power budgets, allowing CPUs to run at higher boost clocks for longer periods. GPUs can also draw more wattage, giving them more headroom for ray tracing and DLSS/FSR upscaling.
